paras: The lynching of Billy LeRoy and his brother was the hanging of an accused stage robber and his brother by vigilantes who took them from the jail at Del Norte, Colorado, in 1881. Both were hanged from a tree by the river hours after LeRoy's capture; the one account found, a correspondent's letter, told it as the end of a famous highwayman.

The letter described LeRoy as a stage-robber chief whose real name was Arthur Pond, 23, of Iowa. According to the correspondent, LeRoy had escaped federal custody after a mail-robbery conviction and was next heard of robbing stages near Del Norte. A Denver report reprinted in August had already linked a June stage robbery between Del Norte and Alamosa with his name.
Captured on a Sunday evening, LeRoy, wounded in the left leg, and his brother were held in the Del Norte jail. Five special deputies were locked in the jail around LeRoy's cell as guards.

Meanwhile a meeting in the principal saloon resolved to "put one desperado out of the way" before his band could rescue him. After midnight more than one hundred vigilantes, "the best citizens and miners" of the region in the letter's words, overpowered the guards and took both prisoners. They hauled the men by wagon to a clump of trees by the river, tied the ropes to a limb, and drew the wagon away.
Coroner Holland, summoned to his window and handed the jail keys, found both bodies among the trees. No report of an inquest verdict or of arrests of the vigilantes appears in the coverage.

The episode survives in one long letter on the front page of the New Dominion of Morgantown, West Virginia, on September 3, 1881, headlined "Hunting a Brigand." The writer, who said he had once been robbed by LeRoy, called him "the dashing highwayman and prince of road agents" and quoted his jests on the way to the tree. It praised the vigilantes yet called the hanging "a climax equally as lawless as his life" and a "shocking death," and it gave neither the victims' race nor a date beyond "a few weeks ago."

accounts.label: Correspondent's letter
accounts.gist: LeRoy and his brother were captured on a Sunday, jailed at Del Norte under guard, and seized after midnight by over one hundred vigilantes who hanged both from a tree by the river; the coroner found the bodies.

framing.detail: Headlined 'Hunting a Brigand. The End of a Western Highwayman's Wild Career,' the letter glamorizes LeRoy and calls the vigilantes 'the best citizens and miners,' while describing the hanging as 'lawless' and a 'shocking death.'

record_check.dossier: No calendar date; a Sunday night, 'a few weeks' before an undated letter printed 1881-09-03. August is plausible but not shown.
Not stated in any report; nothing indicates the victims were Black.
Billy LeRoy (said to be Arthur Pond) and his unnamed brother.

record_check.record: accused of said to have robbed stages
record_check.dossier: LeRoy accused of robbing stages near Del Norte after escaping custody on an earlier mail-robbery conviction; no accusation against the brother is stated.
No county named in the reports; only Del Norte, Colorado.
Three parts of a single letter in one paper (New Dominion, 1881-09-03).

info: Captured on a Sunday shortly before sunset and lynched a few hours past midnight; the letter places it 'a few weeks ago' and gives no calendar date.
Taken from the jail at Del Norte and hanged from a large limb in a clump of trees by the river.
Billy LeRoy, called a highwayman and 'prince of road agents', said to be Arthur Pond, 23, a native of Iowa; and his brother, not named. Race not stated.
LeRoy was said to have been robbing stages near Del Norte after escaping federal custody following a conviction for robbing the mails; no specific charge against the brother is given.
Vigilantes described as 'the best citizens and miners in the region of Del Norte', organized at a meeting in the principal saloon; called a 'vigilance committee'.
